text: Orders have been signed by U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis to deploy more troops to Afghanistan, marking a significant move by President Donald Trump’s administration to address the ongoing conflict, which is now the longest in American history. On Thursday, Mattis disclosed this development but did not provide details regarding the number of troops to be sent, indicating that the additional forces would aid in the fight against Taliban fighters and other militant groups. "Indeed, I have signed orders, but it is not finalized. To clarify, I have authorized some of the troops that will be dispatched, and we are currently determining the specific units," Mattis informed the press. He mentioned that he would refrain from discussing the total number of troops included in the orders until after he briefs Congress next week. However, unnamed U.S. officials have revealed to Reuters that Trump has permitted Mattis to send approximately 4,000 more troops to Afghanistan. "This will involve more advisers, additional enablers, and fire support, for instance," Mattis stated. He further noted that no additional forces had yet been deployed and that the process might take a "couple of days." Following an extensive review of his policy regarding Afghanistan, Trump last week pledged to engage the United States in an indefinite military presence in the nation and vowed to intensify efforts against the Afghan Taliban insurgents. As per Pentagon reports on Wednesday, around 11,000 U.S. personnel are currently stationed in Afghanistan, a figure that exceeds prior estimates. Mattis indicated that the composition of the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan would begin to shift in accordance with Trump’s directives. Even with an increase of several thousand troops, the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan would remain significantly lower than the peak of over 100,000 personnel in 2011, a time when there was considerable domestic political pressure to reduce the expensive military involvement. Some officials expressed skepticism to Reuters about the efficacy of escalating troop numbers, arguing that any politically acceptable figure would likely fall short of making a substantial impact, let alone establishing stability and security. Thus far, over 2,300 American servicemen and women have died, and more than 17,000 have sustained injuries in Afghanistan. The security landscape in the country has worsened for both the U.S. and the Afghan government in recent years. As of February 20, a U.S. military assessment indicated that the Afghan government controlled or had influence over nearly 60 percent of Afghanistan’s 407 districts, reflecting a drop of almost 11 percentage points compared to the same period in 2016, according to data from the U.S. Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction. Earlier in the month, the Taliban warned Trump in an open letter that the military conditions in Afghanistan were "far worse than you realize" and that increasing troop levels would be counterproductive. The Taliban, which aims to re-establish strict Islamic law, has been conducting an insurgency against the Western-supported Afghan government since it was ousted following a U.S.-led invasion after the September 11 attacks in 2001, which were orchestrated by al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden from a location in Afghanistan.
source_text: Mattis signs orders to send additional troops to Afghanistan. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis said on Thursday he had signed orders to send additional troops to Afghanistan, the most concrete step yet by President Donald Trump’s administration in tackling America’s longest war. Mattis did not specify the size of the force, which will help combat Taliban insurgents and other armed Islamists.      “Yes, I have signed orders but it is not complete. In other words I have signed some of the (orders for) troops that will go and we are identifying the specific ones,” Mattis told reporters. Mattis said he would not comment on how many additional troops were included in the orders until he briefs Congress next week, but U.S. officials have told Reuters that Trump has given Mattis the authority to send about 4,000 additional troops to Afghanistan.  “It is more advisers, it is more enablers, fire support, for example,” Mattis said. He added that no additional troops had moved in yet and could take a “couple of days.” After a months-long review of his Afghanistan policy, Trump committed the United States last week to an open-ended conflict in the country and promised a stepped-up campaign against Afghan Taliban insurgents. About 11,000 U.S. troops are serving in Afghanistan, the Pentagon said on Wednesday, thousands more than it has previously stated.     Mattis said that the make up of those U.S. forces in Afghanistan would also start changing in line with Trump’s guidance.  Any increase of several thousand troops would leave U.S. forces in Afghanistan well below their peak of more than 100,000 troops in 2011, when Washington was under huge domestic political pressure to draw down the costly operation. Some U.S. officials have told Reuters they questioned the benefit of sending more troops to Afghanistan because any politically palatable number would not be enough to turn the tide, much less create stability and security. To date, more than 2,300 Americans have been killed and over 17,000 wounded in Afghanistan. The security situation in Afghanistan has deteriorated for the United States and Afghan government over the past few years. The Afghan government was assessed by the U.S. military to control or influence almost 60 percent of Afghanistan’s 407 districts as of Feb. 20, a nearly 11 percentage-point decrease from the same time in 2016, according to data released by the U.S. Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction.  Earlier this month, the Taliban told Trump in an open letter that the military situation in Afghanistan was “far worse than you realize”, and sending in more troops would be self-destructive. The Taliban, seeking to restore strict Islamic law, has waged an insurgency against the Western-backed Afghan government since losing power in a U.S.-led invasion after the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001. Those attacks were planned by al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden from a base in Afghanistan.

text: On Thursday, Turkish authorities apprehended 136 individuals, including former military personnel, teachers, and police officers, in connection with last year's military coup attempt, according to the state-run Anadolu Agency. The operation, which focused on the capital city of Ankara, involved the detention of 60 former security workers and extended across 30 different provinces, Anadolu reported. In a separate initiative that commenced on Wednesday, 55 soldiers were taken into custody in Diyarbakir, with the operation also affecting 26 other provinces, as stated by Anadolu. One additional suspect remains at large. Furthermore, six individuals were arrested in the northern provinces of Samsun and Karabuk, along with 15 teachers who were detained in Ankara, as reported by Anadolu. Allegations against the suspects include their use of the encrypted messaging platform, ByLock, which the government claims was utilized by followers of Fethullah Gulen, a cleric residing in the United States. The Turkish government holds Gulen responsible for the failed coup that occurred in July 2016. Gulen has refuted these accusations and condemned the coup attempt. In the aftermath of the coup in July 2016, over 50,000 individuals, encompassing police, military members, and civil servants, have been imprisoned awaiting trial. Approximately 150,000 individuals have faced dismissal or suspension. This extensive crackdown has raised concerns among Turkey's Western partners and human rights advocates, who argue that President Tayyip Erdogan is leveraging the coup to suppress opposition. The government asserts that the actions taken under emergency regulations imposed after the coup are essential due to the security threats confronting Turkey.
source_text: Turkey detains 136 for suspected ties to coup plotters: agency. ISTANBUL (Reuters) - Turkey detained 136 people, including former police, teachers and soldiers, in four separate operations on Thursday over suspected links to last year s attempted military coup, the state-run Anadolu news agency said. Authorities detained 60 former security officials in the operation centered in the capital Ankara and spread over 30 provinces, Anadolu said. In a separate operation that began on Wednesday and centered on Diyarbakir and spread over 26 other provinces, 55 soldiers were detained, Anadolu said. Officials were still searching for one more suspect. Six others were detained in the northern provinces of Samsun and Karabuk, as well as 15 teachers in Ankara, Anadolu said. The suspects were alleged to be using the encrypted messaging app, ByLock, which the government says was used by the network of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen. Ankara blames Gulen, for orchestrating the failed coup in July 2016. Gulen has denied involvement and denounced the putsch. More than 50,000 people, including police, military personnel and civil servants, have been jailed pending trial in the aftermath of the July 2016 coup. Some 150,000 people were sacked or suspended. The crackdown has alarmed Turkey s Western allies and rights groups, who say President Tayyip Erdogan is using the coup as a pretext to muzzle dissent. The government says the measures, taken under emergency rule that was imposed after the coup, are necessary due to the security threats Turkey faces.

text: A historic military assistance agreement worth $38 billion was signed by the United States and Israel on Wednesday, marking the largest aid package in U.S. history. According to a senior U.S. official, this landmark deal is set to span a decade and will enable Israel, Washington's primary ally in the Middle East, to enhance its fighter aircraft fleet, increase the mobility of its ground forces, and bolster its missile defense capabilities. While this represents the highest amount of military aid ever allocated by the U.S. to any nation, it came with certain concessions from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as confirmed by officials from both governments. These concessions include Israel's commitment to refrain from requesting additional financial support from Congress beyond the annual guarantees outlined in the new agreement, as well as a gradual end to a special arrangement that permitted Israel to allocate a portion of its U.S. aid to its domestic defense industry rather than exclusively on American-made military equipment, as stated by the officials. The lengthy negotiations over the aid, which lasted nearly 10 months, highlighted ongoing tensions between President Barack Obama and Netanyahu regarding the U.S.-led nuclear agreement with Iran, a deal that the Israeli Prime Minister opposed vehemently. Additionally, the two countries have had differences regarding the Palestinian issue. Nevertheless, Netanyahu, who leads a right-wing government, determined that securing a new agreement with Obama, who is set to leave office in January, would be more advantageous than waiting for potentially better terms from the incoming U.S. administration. This new pact allows Netanyahu to circumvent the uncertainties associated with the next president, whether it be Democrat Hillary Clinton or Republican Donald Trump, while providing Israel's military establishment with the stability needed for future planning. In the context of Obama's presidency, his aides viewed reaching a new agreement as a crucial aspect of his legacy before he departs from office. Critics from the Republican party have accused Obama of not being sufficiently attentive to Israel's security concerns, which the White House has firmly refuted, asserting that he has maintained a stringent stance towards the Israeli leader. The memorandum of understanding, valued at $38 billion, covers the U.S. fiscal years from 2019 to 2028, succeeding the $30 billion MOU signed in 2007, which is set to conclude at the end of fiscal year 2018. Obama remarked in a written statement, "Prime Minister Netanyahu and I are confident that the new MOU will make a significant contribution to Israel’s security in what remains a dangerous neighborhood." The signing of the agreement took place at the State Department, where U.S. Undersecretary of State Thomas Shannon and Jacob Nagel, the acting head of Netanyahu’s national security council, finalized the terms. As outlined in a White House "fact sheet," the agreement includes the following components: - annual payments totaling $3.3 billion in foreign military financing - an allocation of $500 million per year specifically for Israeli missile defense programs, marking the first time such funding has been formally included in the aid agreement. - a phased discontinuation of a special provision that has historically allowed Israel to use 26.3 percent of U.S. aid for its own defense sector instead of exclusively on American weapons. - the removal of a longstanding clause permitting Israel to spend approximately 13 percent of U.S. aid on military fuel purchases. - the financial support will enable Israel to modernize the majority of its fighter aircraft, which includes the procurement of additional F-35 Joint Strike Fighters. Israel is set to receive 33 F-35 aircraft, with the first two deliveries expected in December.

text: An airstrike targeted the Qusur area of Deir al-Zor city, which is under government control, resulting in the deaths of over a dozen individuals, according to reports from Syrian state television and a conflict monitoring group. On Monday, state television indicated that the assault was conducted by aircraft from a U.S.-led coalition engaged in combat against the Islamic State, claiming that 14 civilians lost their lives and 32 others sustained injuries. However, a coalition representative stated on Tuesday that they did not execute such an airstrike, noting that their only recent operation in the vicinity occurred across the Euphrates in September. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a monitoring organization based in the UK, mentioned that the identity of the aircraft responsible for the strike remains undetermined, yet they confirmed a higher death toll of at least 22 individuals. The Syrian military, supported by Iran, Russia, and allied Shiite militias, continues to confront the Islamic State in Deir al-Zor and adjacent rural regions. Both Syrian and Russian military aircraft have been targeting Islamic State positions in that region. The coalition, which is backed by U.S. forces, has been carrying out air operations against Islamic State to assist the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), an alliance of Kurdish and Arab fighters, located to the east of Deir al-Zor across the Euphrates River. Clashes have occurred between the U.S.-supported forces and the Syrian army during their respective campaigns against the Islamic State as they attempt to reclaim territory in eastern Syria. Both the United States and Russia have asserted that they maintain communication to avoid potential conflicts between their military efforts.
source_text: Deadly air strike hits Syrian government-held Deir al-Zor: state TV, monitor. BEIRUT (Reuters) - An air raid in the government-held Qusur district of Deir al-Zor city in eastern Syria killed more than a dozen people, Syrian state television and a war monitor said on Monday.  State television said jets from a U.S.-led international coalition battling Islamic State carried out the air strike and that it killed 14 civilians and wounded 32 others.  A spokesman for the coalition said on Tuesday it had not carried out such a raid, and that its only strike in the vicinity in recent weeks took place in September across the Euphrates from the city. The war monitor, the Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, reported that it was not known which aircraft carried out the strike, but that at least 22 people were killed.  The Syrian army, backed by Russia, Iran and Shi ite militias, is fighting Islamic State in the city of Deir al-Zor, as well as in parts of the surrounding countryside. Both Syrian and Russian jets have been hitting Islamic State in that area.  The U.S.-backed coalition has been conducting air strikes against Islamic State in support of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) alliance of Kurdish and Arab militias to the east of Deir al-Zor across the Euphrates.  The rival U.S.-backed and Syrian army offensives against Islamic State have clashed several times over recent months as they have pushed the jihadists from territory in eastern Syria.  The U.S. and Russia have said they communicate with each other to prevent possible points of conflict of violence between the two offensives.

text: On Tuesday, Prime Minister Theresa May's spokesperson stated that the UK believes it can swiftly reach an agreement on a transitional framework for leaving the European Union, even as significant disagreements on the timeline for Brexit remain. The UK is aiming for a so-called implementation period lasting approximately two years after its departure from the EU, which is set for March 2019. During this time, access to the EU single market would largely remain unchanged while new arrangements are established. To eliminate uncertainty regarding future trading regulations, businesses are eager to learn the specifics of such an agreement as soon as possible. We believe that we can quickly agree on the broad outline of an implementation period, the spokesperson remarked, although no additional details were provided regarding the anticipated timeline for reaching this agreement. "We are clear that achieving this implementation period is our goal, and we are confident it can be accomplished. Our priority is to ensure certainty for businesses," he added. However, May caused some confusion among businesses on Monday by stating that any implementation period would not be finalized until an agreement was made concerning the UK's future trading relationship with the EU. This contradicted expectations that a transitional arrangement would be established prior to any trade agreement. It further underscored the stark differences between the UK and the EU regarding the timing of a trade deal. The UK is pursuing an ambitious trade agreement with the EU to supersede its current arrangement once the implementation period concludes. The UK government is confident that its existing close relationship with the EU will facilitate the finalization of such a deal by October 2018. However, Michel Barnier, the EU's chief negotiator, indicated that negotiating a trade agreement would require three years. Consequently, if discussions commence in December, a deal would be ready by the conclusion of a transition period expected to extend until December 2020. When asked whether the UK still held the position that a trade deal could be achieved by the end of the following year within the two-year exit process, the spokesperson replied, "Yes." In response to the timeline proposed by the UK, an official from the EU remarked that the bloc aims to outline a framework for the future relationship by this time next year, ensuring that the withdrawal treaty takes this future relationship into account under the Article 50 legal exit process. However, the official clarified that the EU would only engage in negotiations regarding the specifics of a free trade agreement after the UK has officially exited in March 2019, due to the EU's regulations that prohibit negotiating trade deals with its current members. "Article 50 states that the withdrawal agreement must consider our future relationship, so we will know the terms of our partnership with the EU by the time we exit," a spokeswoman for May stated when inquired about the EU official's position. "However, regarding the specifics, that will be subject to negotiation, and I cannot pre-empt those discussions."

text: U.S. President-elect Donald Trump has demonstrated his recognition of the pressing nature of the nuclear threat from North Korea, as indicated by a statement from South Korea on Tuesday. The South Korean government remarked that Trump's "clear warning" reflects his awareness regarding the dangers posed by North Korea's weapons program and his commitment to maintaining sanctions against the reclusive nation. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un claimed on Sunday that his nation, equipped with nuclear capabilities, was nearing the point of test-launching an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), which could potentially target parts of the United States. In response, Trump dismissed this assertion via a tweet, declaring, "It won’t happen." According to South Korea’s Foreign Ministry, Trump's remarks, which marked his initial reference to the nuclear situation in North Korea since the U.S. elections in November, can be interpreted as a significant "clear warning" directed at the North. Ministry spokesperson Cho June-hyuck mentioned during a press briefing that "due to our proactive engagement, President-elect Trump and U.S. officials are evidently cognizant of the seriousness and immediacy of the North Korean nuclear menace." He added, "They are steadfast in their position on the necessity for sanctions against North Korea and for robust collaboration between South Korea and the U.S." The U.S. State Department acknowledged that North Korea is still advancing its nuclear and missile technologies. State Department spokesperson John Kirby informed journalists, "At this moment, we do not believe he possesses the capability to arm one of these (missiles) with a nuclear warhead ... but we are aware that he is still striving to achieve these capabilities, and the programs continue to progress in that direction." Trump has yet to present a formal policy regarding North Korea; however, during the election campaign, he suggested a willingness to engage in discussions with its leader, Kim, if given the chance. Kellyanne Conway, a spokesperson for Trump, stated on ABC’s "Good Morning America" that the president-elect was "putting North Korea on notice through this tweet and through other statements that this won’t happen." She elaborated, "As the president of the United States, he aims to position himself as a barrier between them and their missile capabilities, which experts indicate could be ready to strike Seattle almost instantly." Conway noted that Trump has not publicly articulated his potential responses to North Korea’s nuclear and missile initiatives and stated, "He won’t do so before his inauguration." "We are aware that there are sanctions available," Conway remarked. "They have not always proven effective. It seems that China would need to play a significant role in this matter as well." Trump has been critical of China concerning this issue. On Monday, he remarked that China has profited from its economic relationship with the United States but has not exerted its influence to manage North Korea. In reaction, Geng Shuang, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry, asserted that China has been advocating for the denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. "China’s initiatives in this area are quite evident," Geng stated during a news briefing. "As a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, we have actively engaged in pertinent discussions concerning the North Korean nuclear dilemma and have collaboratively passed several resolutions with other stakeholders. This reflects China’s responsible stance." When asked about Trump’s opinion that China has not been effective in curbing North Korea’s nuclear ambitions, State Department spokesperson Kirby replied, "We would not concur with that viewpoint." For years, the United States has rebuffed North Korean requests for dialogue, insisting on disarmament as a prerequisite. Both the United States and its ally South Korea have reacted to two nuclear tests and multiple missile tests conducted by North Korea last year with increasingly stringent sanctions. Following Pyongyang’s fifth and most significant nuclear test in September, the U.N. Security Council enacted new sanctions against North Korea at the end of November. A fully developed North Korean ICBM could pose a threat to the continental United States, located approximately 9,000 km (5,500 miles) away from North Korea. source_text: Trump recognizes 'urgency' of North Korea nuclear threat: South Korea. SEOUL/WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. President-elect Donald Trump’s “clear warning” to North Korea shows he is aware of the urgency of the threat posed by North Korea’s nuclear program and will not waver from a policy of sanctions against the isolated country, South Korea said on Tuesday. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said on Sunday his nuclear-capable country was close to test-launching an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), raising the prospect of putting parts of the United States in range. Trump dismissed the claim, saying on Twitter: “It won’t happen.” South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said Trump’s comment, his first mention of the North Korean nuclear issue since the U.S. election in November, could be interpreted as a “clear warning” to the North. “Because of our active outreach, President-elect Trump and U.S. officials are clearly aware of the gravity and urgency of the North Korean nuclear threat,” ministry spokesman Cho June-hyuck said at a briefing. “They are maintaining an unwavering stance on the need for sanctions on North Korea and for close cooperation between South Korea and the U.S.”  The U.S. State Department said it recognized that North Korea continued to pursue nuclear and ballistic missile technologies. “We do not believe that at this point in time he has the capability to tip one of these (missiles) with a nuclear warhead ... but we do know that he continues to want to have those capabilities and the programs continue to march in that direction,” State Department spokesman John Kirby told reporters.    Trump has not outlined a policy on North Korea, but during the U.S. election campaign indicated he would be willing to talk to its leader, Kim, given the opportunity. Trump spokeswoman Kellyanne Conway told ABC’s “Good Morning America” program that the president-elect was “putting North Korea on notice through this tweet and through other statements that this won’t happen.” “He as president of the United States wants to stand between them and their missile capabilities, which experts say could be deployed to reach Seattle almost immediately,” Conway said. She said Trump had not publicly stated how he might respond to North Korea’s nuclear weapons and missile programs and “won’t before he’s inaugurated.” “We do know that there are sanctions that are possible,” Conway said. “They haven’t always worked. I think that China would have to have a significant role here as well.”Trump has been critical of China over the issue. On Monday, he said China had benefited from its economic ties with the United States but would not use its influence to help control North Korea. In response, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Geng Shuang said China had been pushing for the denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. “China’s efforts in this regard are perfectly obvious,” Geng told a news briefing. “As a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council we have proactively participated in relevant discussions on the North Korean nuclear issue and have jointly passed several resolutions with other parties.  “This shows China’s responsible attitude.” Asked about Trump’s view that China was not helping to contain North Korea’s nuclear ambitions, the State Department’s Kirby said: “We would not agree with that assessment.” The United States has for years dismissed North Korean calls for talks, insisting it must disarm first.  The United States and ally South Korea have responded to two North Korean nuclear tests and various missile tests last year with ever-more-severe sanctions. The U.N. Security Council imposed new sanctions on North Korea at the end of November after Pyongyang carried out its fifth and largest nuclear test so far in September. A North Korean ICBM, once fully developed, could threaten the continental United States, which is about 9,000 km (5,500 miles) from the North.  ICBMs have a minimum range of about 5,500 km (3,400 miles), but some are designed to travel 10,000 km (6,200 miles) or further.     North Korea worked last year on developing components for an ICBM, saying it was close to a test-launch plausible, international weapons experts said on Monday.

text: The U.S. Supreme Court showed signs on Wednesday of being inclined to allow property owners to contest federal permit requirements under a national water protection statute in a case related to a Minnesota peat mining initiative. During a one-hour session, the justices deliberated on the delicate equilibrium between property rights and environmental regulations, specifically referencing the pivotal U.S. Clean Water Act from 1972. A significant portion of the eight justices seemed to lean toward the position of Hawkes Co Inc, a company based in North Dakota, which is challenging an Obama administration determination that its land contains wetlands. The legislation requires property owners to obtain permits in such scenarios. For developers and landowners, determining whether a specific area falls within the law's oversight is crucial, as this designation initiates a drawn-out and costly permitting procedure. The attorneys representing Hawkes contended that the firm ought to have the right to dispute whether it is obligated to navigate the permitting process. Justices from both sides of the political spectrum voiced worries regarding the existing system's impact on property owners. Chief Justice John Roberts, who is conservative, remarked that applicants ignoring a government determination requiring a permit are at “great practical risk.” Liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg described the current process as “very arduous and very expensive.” Justice Stephen Breyer, also a liberal, asserted that the government’s conclusion that Hawkes required a permit was “perfectly suited for review in the courts.” Only Justice Elena Kagan, representing the liberal ideologies, showed support for the government, expressing worries about the consequences that a verdict favoring property owners could have on other governmental bodies, such as the Securities and Exchange Commission. Advocates for property rights indicated that the permitting process can extend up to two years and incur costs reaching $270,000, with potential fines of up to $37,500 per day for noncompliance. Various business organizations, including the National Association of Home Builders and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, along with 29 states, submitted legal documents opposing the Obama administration in this matter. This case follows a unanimous ruling by the justices in 2012, which established that property owners facing enforcement actions under the Clean Water Act could seek judicial intervention prior to being compelled to comply or face financial penalties. Last year, the Obama administration introduced a new regulation that clarified the extent of federal authority over aquatic bodies. However, a federal appeals court suspended this rule after it was contested by 18 states. With Justice Antonin Scalia's passing in February, only eight justices are involved in this case. A decision is anticipated by the conclusion of June.

A majority of the eight justices appeared sympathetic toward North Dakota-based Hawkes Co Inc, which is fighting an Obama administration finding that its property includes wetlands. The law mandates that property owners get permits in such situations. Whether a particular plot of land falls under the law’s jurisdiction is important to developers and other property owners because such a finding triggers a lengthy and expensive permitting process. Hawkes’ lawyers argued the company should be able to contest whether it even needs to go through the permit process. Liberal and conservative justices alike expressed concern about the current arrangement’s burden on property owners. Conservative Chief Justice John Roberts said applicants who disregard a government finding that they need a permit do so at “great practical risk.” Liberal Ruth Bader Ginsburg called the process “very arduous and very expensive.” Liberal Stephen Breyer called the government decision that Hawkes needed a permit “perfectly suited for review in the courts.” Only liberal Elena Kagan expressed support for the government, raising concerns about the impact a ruling favoring property owners would have on actions by other government agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission. Property rights advocates said the permitting process can take two years and cost up to $270,000, with owners facing penalties of up to $37,500 a day for noncompliance. Business groups including the National Association of Home Builders and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and 29 states filed court papers opposing the Obama administration in the case. The case follows the justices’ unanimous 2012 ruling that property owners facing enforcement action under the Clean Water Act can ask a court to intervene before being forced to comply or pay financial penalties. The Obama administration last year issued a new regulation defining the scope of federal jurisdiction over bodies of water. A federal appeals court put the rule on hold after it was challenged by 18 states. Only eight justices participated in the case following Justice Antonin Scalia’s February death. A ruling is due by the end of June.

text: Court documents have revealed that Paul Manafort, the former campaign manager for President Donald Trump who is facing indictment, spent nearly $1 million on a collection of rugs within a span of two years, in addition to over $1.3 million on clothing from high-end retailers in Beverly Hills, California, and New York City. His extravagant way of living, which included residences in Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Hamptons, and Arlington, Virginia, was outlined in an indictment submitted to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, which came to light on Monday. The indictment, brought forth by Justice Department Special Counsel Robert Mueller, indicated that Manafort “utilized his concealed wealth from abroad to indulge in an extravagant lifestyle in the United States.” Prosecutors reported that they uncovered payments made by Manafort for four Range Rovers and a Mercedes-Benz, which they alleged were illegally derived from overseas funds to evade U.S. income tax responsibilities, as detailed in the 31-page court filing. Additionally, evidence emerged that Manafort purchased a condominium in a refurbished red-brick building situated in the upscale Soho district of New York City for $2.85 million, also from foreign funds, primarily sourced from Cyprus. On Monday, both Manafort and his associate Rick Gates entered not guilty pleas to charges of money laundering and other offenses as part of an investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. During the court proceedings, both Manafort and Gates maintained a stoic demeanor. A federal prosecutor from Mueller’s team, Greg Andres, remarked that his office faced challenges in accurately assessing the net worth of Manafort and Gates, complicating the process of establishing appropriate bail terms. According to Andres, Manafort reported a diverse range of net asset values on various financial documents and loans, indicating figures as low as $20 million and as high as $100 million. Gates, in contrast, provided figures ranging from $2 million to $30 million. As a result, a federal judge mandated house arrest for both individuals, setting a $10 million unsecured bond for Manafort and a $5 million unsecured bond for Gates. Kevin Downing, Manafort’s attorney, stated on Monday that there was no proof indicating that his client collaborated with the Russian government during his time on the Trump campaign. The indictment made no mention of Trump or his campaign. Manafort led the Trump campaign from June to August in 2016, resigning amid allegations of receiving millions in illegal payments from a pro-Russian political party in Ukraine. The indictment asserted that both Manafort and Gates generated tens of millions of dollars from work in Ukraine and laundered funds through numerous U.S. and foreign entities to conceal payments from American authorities. It was noted in the indictment that Manafort spent $849,215 at a men’s clothing store in New York and $520,440 at a Beverly Hills store. Furthermore, he acquired a house in Water Mill, New York, within Long Island’s Hamptons for $5,434,793, also investing $820,240 in landscaping. Aerial images of the property reveal a garden, a swimming pool, a tennis court, a basketball court, and a putting green along with a sand trap, all situated on 2.37 acres (0.96 hectare). Additionally, a seven-bedroom brownstone in Brooklyn, purchased for $3 million, was characterized in a real estate listing as “dripping with detail - perfectly intact crown moldings and medallions, gold leafed carved window detail, 5 marble mantels, and original Lincrusta paper wall covering.”
